_link.title: I can calculate the radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a magnetic field using qvB = mv²/r

toLevel2.stem: Which formula gives the radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a magnetic field?
distractors: r = qB/(mv)
r = qvB/m
r = mB/(qv)

toLevel2.stem: The equation qvB = mv²/r is derived by equating which two forces?
distractors: Gravitational force and electric force
Magnetic force and gravitational force
Centripetal force and frictional force

toLevel2.stem: According to r = mv/(qB), what happens to the radius if the mass of the particle is doubled?
distractors: The radius halves
The radius stays the same
The radius quadruples

toLevel2.stem: According to r = mv/(qB), what happens to the radius if the magnetic field strength is doubled?
distractors: The radius doubles
The radius stays the same
The radius quadruples

toLevel2.stem: Which quantity does NOT appear in the radius formula r = mv/(qB)?
distractors: Mass of the particle
Charge of the particle
Speed of the particle

toLevel2.stem: The radius of the circular path is given by r = {{blank:1}} / ({{blank:2}}).
A heavier particle follows a {{blank:1}} circle, while a stronger magnetic field produces a {{blank:2}} circle.
The radius formula is derived by setting the {{blank:1}} force equal to the {{blank:2}} force.
A faster charged particle follows a circular path with a larger radius in the same magnetic field.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Increasing the charge of a particle increases the radius of its circular path.
distractors: True

toLevel3.stem: Why does a faster particle follow a larger circle in the same magnetic field?
toLevel3.answer: The magnetic force increases with speed but the centripetal acceleration needed increases faster (v²/r), requiring a larger radius
distractors: A faster particle has more charge so the magnetic force pushes it to a wider orbit
A faster particle has more mass so it needs more force to change its direction of travel
The magnetic field weakens when a particle moves faster through it causing less deflection

toLevel3.stem: Why does a stronger magnetic field produce a smaller radius for the same particle at the same speed?
toLevel3.answer: A stronger field exerts a greater force, providing more centripetal acceleration for a tighter curve
distractors: A stronger field slows the particle down, so it needs less space to complete a full circle
A stronger field increases the particle's mass, which makes it curve more tightly in circles
A stronger field reduces the charge on the particle causing it to follow a smaller radius

toLevel3.stem: Two particles have the same charge and speed but different masses. Which has the larger radius?
toLevel3.answer: The heavier particle, because radius is proportional to mass
distractors: The lighter particle, because less mass is easier to deflect
Both have the same radius because mass does not appear
The heavier particle, because it has a larger charge value

toLevel3.stem: An electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s in a 0.020 T field. What is the radius?
In a mass spectrometer, how does measuring the radius of a particle's path allow identification of the particle?
toLevel3.answer: The radius depends on mass, so particles of different masses follow different radii
distractors: The radius depends on charge only, so different charges hit different detector points
The radius is the same for all particles, so identification uses time of flight instead
The radius depends on speed only, so faster particles are identified by larger circles

toLevel3.stem: If both the speed and the field strength are doubled, what happens to the radius?
toLevel3.answer: The radius stays the same because the effects cancel
distractors: The radius doubles because speed has a stronger effect
The radius halves because field has a stronger effect
The radius quadruples because both effects multiply

toLevel3.stem: In r = mv/(qB), the radius is directly proportional to {{blank:1}} and inversely proportional to {{blank:2}}.
A mass spectrometer identifies particles by their {{blank:1}} because particles with different {{blank:2}} follow circles of different radii.
Doubling the speed of a particle {{blank:1}} the radius, while doubling the charge {{blank:2}} the radius.
A particle with twice the charge follows a circle with twice the radius at the same speed and field.
distractors: True

toLevel4.stem: A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m/s in a 0.50 T field. Calculate the radius.

An alpha particle (m = 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) and a proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enter the same field at the same speed. What is the ratio of their radii (r_alpha / r_proton)?
A particle follows a circular path of radius 0.12 m in a 0.40 T field. If the field is reduced to 0.10 T, what is the new radius?
An ion of unknown mass has charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, speed 1.0 × 10⁵ m/s, and curves with radius 0.21 m in a 0.050 T field. What is the mass of the ion?
Two isotopes of the same element have masses 20 u and 22 u. They enter a mass spectrometer with the same speed and charge. What is the ratio of their radii?

An engineer wants a particle to follow a circle of radius exactly 1.0 m. Given m = 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and v = 1.0 × 10⁷ m/s, what field strength is needed?
To find the mass of an unknown ion in a mass spectrometer, rearrange to m = {{blank:1}} / {{blank:2}}.
The ratio of radii for two isotopes with the same charge and speed equals the ratio of their {{blank:1}}, allowing the spectrometer to {{blank:2}} them.
To achieve a desired radius, an engineer can adjust the {{blank:1}} strength; increasing it will {{blank:2}} the radius.

toLevel5.stem: A student derives r = mv/(qB) and concludes that radius is independent of the direction of the magnetic field. Evaluate this conclusion.
toLevel5.answer: The magnitude of the radius is independent of field direction, but the direction of curvature depends on the field orientation
distractors: The conclusion is entirely correct; neither the radius nor the curvature direction depends on field direction
The conclusion is wrong; reversing the field would double the radius of the circular path
The conclusion is wrong; the formula only works when the field points in one specific direction

toLevel5.stem: Compare the usefulness of r = mv/(qB) for identifying particles in a mass spectrometer versus a time-of-flight detector.
toLevel5.answer: The radius formula separates particles spatially by mass; time-of-flight separates them temporally by speed differences
distractors: The radius formula is always superior because it does not depend on the particle's speed value
Time-of-flight is always superior because it can measure any particle regardless of its charge
Both methods give identical results and are completely interchangeable in all applications

toLevel5.stem: In a synchrotron, the magnetic field strength is increased as particles accelerate. Using r = mv/(qB), explain why this is necessary.
toLevel5.answer: As speed increases, B must increase proportionally to keep the radius constant for the fixed-size ring
distractors: Increasing B is needed to increase the particle's charge so it stays in the correct orbit
Increasing B is needed to reduce the particle's mass so it can travel faster in the ring
Increasing B decreases the radius, which is needed because the ring shrinks during operation

toLevel5.stem: An ion has mass m and charge q. Another ion has mass 2m and charge 2q. Compare their radii at the same speed and field.
toLevel5.answer: Both have the same radius because the ratio m/q is the same for both ions
distractors: The heavier ion has twice the radius because mass has a stronger effect than charge
The lighter ion has twice the radius because it has less charge deflecting it inward
The heavier ion has half the radius because its larger charge creates more deflection

toLevel5.stem: Analyse the limitations of using r = mv/(qB) at speeds approaching the speed of light.
toLevel5.answer: At relativistic speeds, the effective mass increases, so the actual radius is larger than the classical formula predicts
distractors: The formula remains perfectly accurate at all speeds including those near the speed of light
At relativistic speeds the charge decreases, making the radius smaller than the formula predicts
The formula breaks down because magnetic fields cannot act on particles near the speed of light

toLevel5.stem: A mass spectrometer measures radii of 0.150 m and 0.165 m for two singly charged ions at the same speed and field. Calculate the ratio of their masses.
A student claims that since r = mv/(qB), you can determine both the mass and the charge of an unknown particle from a single radius measurement. Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; only the ratio m/q can be determined from a single radius measurement at known v and B
distractors: Correct; the mass and charge can both be calculated independently from the radius alone
Incorrect; neither the mass nor the charge can be determined from the radius of the path
Correct; but only if the speed of the particle is also measured at the same time as radius

toLevel5.stem: Predict how the radius of an electron's path in a magnetic field compares to a proton's path at the same kinetic energy (not speed) and field.
toLevel5.answer: The electron's radius is much smaller because at the same kinetic energy it has far less momentum than the proton
distractors: The radii are the same because kinetic energy and momentum are always proportional for all particles
The electron's radius is larger because it moves much faster at the same kinetic energy value
The proton's radius is smaller because its greater mass produces more centripetal force overall

toLevel5.stem: In a synchrotron, B is increased in proportion to {{blank:1}} to maintain a constant {{blank:2}} as particles accelerate.
A single radius measurement in a mass spectrometer determines the {{blank:1}} of an ion, not the mass and charge {{blank:2}}.
